Mugabe Falls

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Robert Mugabe resigne as president after 37 years of brutal autocracy - but what now for Zimbabwe?

Unique Selling Point:
In the news event of the year, Zimbabwe's Robert Mugabe resigned after a bloodless coup by the army, saw thousands of people take to the streets in spontaneous jubilation. But what now for the region? Did the Army Commander Chiwenga's visit to China only a week beforehand give them the confidence to act? What is China's influence on the country?
Will the former Vice President Emmerson Mnangagwa return the country to democracy, or will his bloody past as leader of the Central Intelligence Organization , and architect of the Matabeleland Massacres, be the blueprint for the future?

Summary:
It's estimated that between 1 and 3 million Zimbabweans are living in South Africa. As the euphoria subsides, will they rush home and build a new Zimbabwe, or will they bide their time and wait to see if the future of their country is stable?

Press Release:


Mugabe Falls
As millions of Zimbabweans celebrated the resignation of Robert Mugabe as President of Zimbabwe,
Emmerson Mnangagwa, Mugabe’s former right–hand fist, prepares to take over the reins as interim
president of the country. But will he return the country to democracy, or will his past as leader of the
Central Intelligence Organization and architect of the Matabeleland massacres be the blueprint for the
future?

Script:


MUGABE FALLS


Emmerson: “I will devote myself to the wellbeing of Zimbabwe and its people, so help me God/”

V/O: The Presidential inauguration of Emmerson Mnangagwa ended a momentous week in the history of Zimbabwe. Only last Saturday, the people took to the streets in unprecedented protests against Robert Mugabe’s tyranny.
03:10
Trevor: What you saw on Saturday is an overflow of pent-up frustration and anger.

V/O: Trevor Ncube is a Zimbabwean entrepreneur and newspaper publisher.

Trevor: What Robert Mugabe has done over the past 37 years is beyond criminal. Families were torn apart, dreams shattered, businesses destroyed, people killed, just because this man wanted to hold on until he drops dead.

V/O: Last Sunday night, Mugabe’s much-anticipated resignation failed to materialise, and it seemed it seemed like the old man would never go.

Biti: He never was a President for Zimbabweans, he was always president of ZANU-PF.

V/O: Tendai Biti is a former Minister of Finance in Zimbabwe.

Biti: In the last 5 months, it was clear that he wasn’t even president of the ZANU-PF, he was president of the Mugabe dynasty. And that is what he was concerned with: Mugabe, Mugabe, and nothing else except Mugabe.

V/O: The generals were at pains to avoid a coup, and follow the Constitution.
08:50
Alex: We’ve had this very gentle process, almost you know so genteel you felt that the generals are having tea and scones with President Mugabe at his house at one moment.

V/O: Dr Alex Vines is the Head of the Africa Programme at Chatham House, the London think tank of the Royal Institute of International Affairs.
09::10
Alex: What they wanted is a constitutionally-backed, transitional process, which is what has occurred.

V/O: But not so, says Zimbabwean constitutional law expert, and independent politician, Fadzayi Mahere.

Fadzayi: It’s definitely not constitutional. The Constitution does not have space, does not provide for a situation where the military intervenes in political affairs. The military has no place in the transfer of power.

V/O: Nevertheless Zanu-PF fired Mugabe as party chief, expelled first lady Grace, and named Mnangagwa as party leader. On Tuesday Parliament convened in the ballroom of the Rainbow Towers Hotel to begin impeachment proceedings. But shortly before the debate began, a letter was delivered to the Speaker, Jacob Mudenda.

Jacob: “A letter from the President: notice of resignation.”

Sfx: Cheering in parliament

V/O: Jubilation erupted on the streets of Harare as almost 4 decades of repression came to an end. Zimbabweans celebrated loudly into the night, and the Mugabes could not have escaped the cacophony.

Fadzayi: If a Constitution is an expression of the will of the people, one has to say that once that will is expressed in such a strong way – especially after one person mangling and twisting the Constitution to suit his own ends, one has to say it’s right.

Link: Shortly before the momentous events in Zimababwe, the head of the Army, General Constantino Chiwenga, went to China. That visit has raised questions about the possible influence of the Chinese on this soft coup.
05:00
Alex: They weren't going to say yes, go ahead and stage a coup. But they probably said well if there is political change in Zimbabwe and it results in a more enabling business environment, then there could be more Chinese loans for Zimbabwe. I think that’s probably the way the conversation would have gone.

V/O: It’s reported the Mugabe’s have been granted full immunity to stay in Zimbabwe, but what about the other Ministers who were arrested by the military?

Trevor: We don’t know the whereabouts of Jonathan Moyo; we don’t know the whereabouts of Saviour Kasukuwere, we don’t know the whereabouts of Robert Mugabe’s nephew Patrick Zhuwao.

V/O: On Friday, the military handed over former Finance Minister Ignatius Chombo, to the police.

Link: Emmerson Mnangagwa is now the President of Zimababwe, and while the country celebrates this transition, his role in its brutal past cannot be forgotten. For some, this change is a snake shedding its skin.

Trevor: Mnangagwa is feared because of his background in intelligence. Mnangagwa is feared because of Gukurahundi, 20 000 Zimbabweans in Matebeleland were killed.

V/O: The Matabeleland Massacres were followed by election violence in 2002 and 2008.

Biti: I was tortured in 2008. They did terrible things to me which I can’t say without crying. But you cannot move forward without making peace with the past, but it doesn’t mean the past should imprison the future.

Fadzayi: You know, the most powerful words that we can hear right now from Mr Emmerson Mnangagwa is “I’m sorry, and me and my generals are sorry, and those who have been in power are sorry. How can we go forward?”

V/O: In his inaugural speech the President didn’t quite apologise, but alluded to mistakes of the past.

Prez: We should never remain hostages of our past. I thus humbly appeal to all of us that we let bygones be bygones.”

V/O: Zimbabwean Jamie Mighti is a final year law student at Wits University.

Jamie: I think trying to bury Gukurahundi, trying to bury political atrocities as if Mnangagwa wasn’t there as a co-star to that atrocity is intellectually dishonest, and in fact it may be us just getting caught up in the euphoria, and not thinking about the post-Mugabe era.

Link: It is unclear how many Zimbabweans are currently living in South Africa - estimates say around 1 to 3 million people - and now that change has come, will they want to pack up and go home?

Lloyd: For now, it’s a wait and see situation.

Taps: 100% I want to go back home, but we need money so that we can go back home and restart.

Lloyd: We just wait and hear his speech on the inauguration. What is he going to say, his plans?

Link: When the dust settles and the euphoria dissipates, what is the future of Zimbabwe? The reality is they’re faced with a 95% unemployment rate, and 85% of the population survives on less than R5 a day.

Trevor: I would love us to regain our status as the bread basket of the continent. We can do it, we’ve got the skills, we’ve got the raw materials, we’ve got the resources for us to do that. We have been poorly led, it’s about time we stand up as citizens to ensure that we are properly led.
07:20
Fadzayi: Dictatorship is a product of a citizenry that doesn’t participate, that is afraid to engage, doesn’t want to get involved. That is what creates bad leaders. And so, for it to sustainably for the long term ensure that Zimbabwe never slumps into a dictatorship again, people need to be educated on their constitutional rights,

Biti: We have removed a baobab, so we are not going to allow another small tree to sink its roots in our country and become another baobab.

Jamie: They say you can’t teach an old dog new tricks, I’m not convinced you can teach an old crocodile new tricks either.

V/O: For now, President Mnangagwa has promised to restore the economy, and hold democratic elections next year.

Prez: “I commit to you today that these elections will be held as scheduled.”
